name: Mak (China)
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: 5. 聲調：莫話共有七個聲調，其中一個少見，且多在借字中出現。[...] 6. 輕聲：有些字如語助詞，及複合詞之前一個字，及一句中意義不重的字皆可輕讀。輕讀時有兩個調 (1) 半高，在字前加高點，如 ˙tə k'un 路上，˙ti ka:u 原處，(2) 半低，在字前加低點，如 .tə ma 馬，.lə ʐa:u 女婿。有些字讀時雖輕，但仍不失其原來聲調，只音調低些及音程縮小而已，這可以叫作半輕讀。這類字除字前加低點外，後仍附調號 [...]。這類字多輕重兩可。本篇材料收集時說話相當的慢，因此也許有許多輕讀的字變成半輕讀了。
new_statements.translation: 5. Tones: Mak has seven tones in all, one of which is rare and occurs mostly in loanwords. [...] 6. Light (unstressed) syllables: some words, such as grammatical particles, the first member of a compound word, and words of little semantic weight in a sentence, may all be read lightly (unstressed). When read lightly there are two pitches: (1) half-high, marked with a raised dot before the syllable, e.g. ˙tə k'un 'on the road', ˙ti ka:u 'original place'; (2) half-low, marked with a low dot, e.g. .tə ma 'horse', .lə ʐa:u 'son-in-law'. Some words, though read lightly, still do not lose their original tone; only the pitch is somewhat lower and the pitch range compressed; this may be called half-light reading. Such words, besides the low dot in front, still carry their tone mark [...]. Words of this class can mostly be read either light or heavy. When this material was collected the speech was rather slow, so perhaps many light syllables became half-light.
new_statements.citation: Li Fang-kuei 李方桂. 1948. 莫話記略 (Notes on Mak Language). Bulletin of the Institute of History and Philology, Academia Sinica 19: 1-80.

I rendered PDF pages 2, 6 and 7 myself with page render (independently of the other reader's saved JPGs) and read the page images directly (no chi_tra scanned model on the box; eng only). PDF p.7 = printed p.7, running head 莫話記略. Section 5 聲調 opens exactly '莫話共有七個聲調，其中一個少見，且多在借字中出現。' followed by the seven tones (1)低升調... (7)高平調 ('此調少見，多是漢語近來借字'). Section 6 輕聲 reads, character for character as quoted: '有些字如語助詞，及複合詞之前一個字，及一句中意義不重的字皆可輕讀。輕讀時有兩個調 (1) 半高，在字前加高點，如 ˙tə k'un 路上，˙ti ka:u 原處，(2) 半低，在字前加低點，如.tə ma 馬，.lə ʐa:u 女婿。有些字讀時雖輕，但仍不失其原來聲調，只音調低些及音程縮小而已，這可以叫作半輕讀。這類字除字前加低點外，後仍附調號，如 ma.ʔe. pa:i lun na ˙li 我媽上舅舅家去了。這類字多輕重兩可。本篇材料收集時說話相當的慢，因此也許有許多輕讀的字變成半輕讀了。'…
new_statements.translation_language: Chinese (traditional characters; Chao tone letters after the romanised examples omitted in the quote)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mak is a seven-tone language; the description gives no fixed word-stress position. What it states is a destressing rule: particles, the first syllable of compound words (i.e. prefix-like minor syllables such as tə-, lə-, ti-), and semantically light words may be unstressed, in which case the syllable loses its lexical tone and surfaces with a neutral half-high or half-low pitch and a short central vowel; a weaker grade ('half-light') keeps the tone with lowered, compressed pitch. By implication full (stressed, tone-bearing) syllables are the final members of such compounds, but the source does not phrase this as 'stress on the last syllable'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; only a three-way grading full / half-light (半輕讀, tone kept but compressed) / light (輕讀, tone lost).
new_statements.exceptions: Destressing is optional ('這類字多輕重兩可' - most such words can be read light or heavy); the author warns that slow elicitation tempo probably turned many light syllables into half-light ones. Tone 7 (high level) is rare and mostly in recent Chinese loans.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement covers both word level (first element of compounds, noun-prefix syllables) and sentence level (particles, semantically light words in a sentence); examples are phrases and sentences from connected texts. Variety: Fangcun 方村 Mak, Libo county (one consultant, about one week of fieldwork in 1942).
new_statements.identity_note: Li 1948 describes the Fangcun 方村 variety of Mak (Libo county, NW), explicitly excluding other Mak-speaking areas and the separate 'Cham' (Ai-Cham, aich1238) of Boyao; Glottolog makc1235 'Mak (China)' covers this. Ni 1988 (wishlist) describes the Yangfeng 陽鳳 dialect instead. Note Glottolog lists the 1948 BIHP item as written in English; it is in Chinese with an English title only.

sources.note: Section (二)音韵 has 5.聲調 (seven tones, one rare and mostly in Chinese loans) and a dedicated 6.輕聲 (p.7): particles, the FIRST element of a compound word, and semantically light words in a sentence may be read unstressed (輕讀); an unstressed syllable loses its tone and takes one of two pitches (half-high, marked with a raised dot; half-low, marked with a low dot); some are only 'half-light' (keep their tone with lowered, compressed pitch); 'such words can mostly be read either light or heavy'. p.6 adds that short ə is the vowel of unstressed syllables. No statement of a fixed stress position; no…
